companyRankingLists.itemDescription: The newly created aerospace giant emerged in April 2020 from the merger of United Technologies and Raytheon Co. Former UT CEO Greg Hayes took over as chief executive, while Raytheon boss Thomas Kennedy became the board’s executive chairman. The pair focused the new company on winning more government orders, including a $320 million NASA contract to support operations at the International Space Station. It was a strategy created partly out of necessity, because Raytheon’s other major customer base—the commercial airline industry—was decimated by the pandemic. The company laid off 16,500 workers and cut costs by $2 billion; even so, operating profits at Raytheon’s two aerospace units dropped 67% and 131% in 2020 compared with the prior year.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
The parcel delivery giant reported revenue of $93.5 billion (up 11.4%) and profits of $3.8 billion (down 26.9%). Rajesh Subramaniam succeeded founder Frederick Smith as CEO on June 1, 2022.

  • In February 2023, FedEx cut 10% of global officer and director jobs, a cost-cutting move prompted in part by diminishing revenue from e-commerce.

  • Subramaniam announced in April 2023 that FedEx would combine its express and ground businesses. Smith had long defended keeping the units separate, even as analysts and investors urged their merger to simplify operations. Subramaniam says the move will help consumers understand pricing and shipping options more easily.

  • FedEx is the fourth largest employer on the Fortune 500.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: As one of the largest delivery services companies in the U.S., FedEx has employed thousands of workers on the front lines of the pandemic. To support them, the company debuted a new health care advocate program called Choose Well Care Connect, which provides those workers with a single point of contact whenever they have a health care need, helping them navigate a complex system of vendors. It’s also made 24/7 confidential counseling available to all employees, eligible dependents, and household members, even if they aren’t actively participating in the plan. The company facilitates career advancement through the FedEx Learning Center, which offers over 25,000 online courses; Aspire, which provides hourly employees access to experiential learning, coaching, and development opportunities; and direct tuition assistance for higher education. “I greatly appreciate the mentoring and guidance the managers at FedEx offer to everyone,” says one staffer. “I feel there is a sense of caring from management to their employees.”

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Second only to United Parcel Service in the package-shipping business, FedEx grew faster than its rival in 2019. The delivery dynamo brought in nearly $69.7 billion in its most recent fiscal year, up 6.5% from FY 2018. Still, FedEx investors despaired over a once marquee customer, Amazon, turning to a competitor. Readying itself for the fight of its life, FedEx spent big sums to revamp its delivery network, known primarily for catering to businesses, to go the “last mile” and drop off boxes on residential doorsteps. Costly investments, in part, caused profits to plummet more than 88%, to $540 million. On a December earnings call, FedEx’s chief financial officer described the hit as “horrific.” But instead of slashing costs, FedEx has swelled its ranks, adding nearly 30,000 more employees over the past year.

  • Auto claims stabilized in 2022 after first dropping in 2020 because of stay-at-home initiatives and then jumping up in 2021 as drivers returned to the road.

  • Progressive is one of the 52 Fortune 500 companies that have women leaders, with Tricia Griffith as president and CEO. Progressive is one of the few companies with a female board chair: Lawton W. Fitt, a retired Goldman Sachs partner.

Energy Transfer, the largest operator of natural gas pipelines in the U.S. by revenue, reported $89.9 billion in revenue in 2022, a 33% increase from the previous year, boosting it 11 spots on this year’s list.

  • In 2022 Energy Transfer signed 20-year deals for the sale of liquefied natural gas with London-based oil company Shell and commodities trader Gunvor’s Singapore trading desk for 2.1 million tonnes a year and 2 million tonnes a year, respectively.

  • Energy Transfer announced the $1.45 billion purchase of Lotus Midstream in March 2023, following a series of smaller acquisitions in 2022 worth $1.1 billion.

  • The company faced several adverse legal outcomes in 2022: Pennsylvania’s attorney general found it criminally liable for repeatedly allowing industrial waste to flow into residential areas, while the Supreme Court upheld a judgment forcing Energy Transfer’s Sunoco unit to pay 53,000 oil well owners in Oklahoma $155 million for interest on late payments.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Texas-based midstream energy company Energy Transfer jumped 27 spots on this year’s list, with revenue increasing 73% to $67.4 billion and profits up 89%, to $5.5 billion. Its improved performance is in part due to higher commodity prices and increased natural gas liquid (NGL) transportation and export volumes, all driven by the rebounding global economy. In December 2021, Energy Transfer finalized its acquisition of Enable Midstream Partners—adding significant natural gas and oil infrastructure assets to its portfolio. A strengthened domestic pipeline network gives the company better odds of weathering any instability in the global energy market resulting from the war in Ukraine.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: With public spaces closed throughout 2020, and demand for heat and electricity down, Dallas, Texas-based pipeline operator Energy Transfer saw revenues drop 28% to just under $39 billion; the business fell 105 spots on the Global 500 as a result. But shortly after the close of its 2020 fiscal year, the company, whose pipelines carry about a third of U.S. crude and natural gas, got a controversial boost: The winter storm that ground Texas to a halt in early 2021 led Energy Transfer to rake in an extra $2 billion. As much of the state of 29 million people went without gas and electricity, demand for supplies from the company’s storage facilities soared. That profit attracted a lawsuit from utility CPS Energy, arguing that prices for natural gas during the deadly storm were 15,000% higher than usual; tragedy shouldn’t be a “jackpot” for a business, the utility said. In a statement, Energy Transfer said it sold the gas to CPS Energy "at a fully negotiated and transparent price of which they were fully aware before receiving and consuming the gas."

companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
The consumer packaged goods giant Procter & Gamble, famous for products ranging from Tide detergent to Pepto Bismol, saw revenue increase 5% in 2022, to $80.2 billion.

  • As inflation raged in 2022 and into 2023, P&G was among the most prominent companies criticized by consumer activists for “greedflation,” as it repeatedly raised prices for consumers in attempts to offset its own rising costs.

  • P&G raised its year-end sales outlook in April 2023 from a 1% decline to a 1% increase, a sign it believes it’s turned the corner on inflation.

  • The company is diversifying away from traditional retail channels; its e-commerce sales grew 11% in 2022 and now make up 14% of total sales.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Procter & Gamble makes and sells familiar household brands such as Tide laundry detergent, Gillette razors, Crest toothpaste, and Old Spice deodorant. Like other consumer goods giants, P&G has faced a tricky balancing act: It is benefiting from rising sales in a recovering economy (it brought in $76.1 billion in revenue in its last fiscal year, a 7.3% increase from the year prior) while also striving to protect its profit margins from inflation. The company also faced a potential self-inflicted wound going into 2022: The detection of benzene, a potential carcinogen, in some of its aerosol deodorants led P&G to institute a recall in November 2021, and the problem has since prompted multiple lawsuits.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: The consumer products giant emerged from the COVID-19 crisis with strong profits, exceeding its own fiscal year 2020 goals with 6% organic sales growth and 13% core earnings-per-share growth. That was partially thanks to a spike in demand for home-goods brands like Charmin, Bounty, Downy, and more. Procter & Gamble experienced a substantial leap in revenue almost across the board, including net sales of $19.7 billion in the second quarter of fiscal year 2021, up 8% from the year before. P&G’s share price has weathered market volatility, rising 15.4% from March 2, 2020, through May 24, 2021. The company even increased its quarterly dividend by 10% in April 2021, making this the 65th consecutive year that P&G has boosted its dividend.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
Sysco, a food marketer and distributor, jumped up 14 spots on the Fortune 500 and posted a 34% increase in revenue in 2022, as restaurant demand—abnormally low during the height of the pandemic—rebounded.

  • The majority of Sysco's sales come from operations in the U.S., but international growth outstripped domestic in 2022, partly due to the reversal of more stringent pandemic restrictions abroad.

  • The company sued a slew of meat companies in 2022, alleging that they violated antitrust regulations through price fixing. Although Sysco moved to settle the lawsuits, it is now mired in a legal battle with Burford Capital, which financed Sysco’s litigation.

  • The workforce for the food marketer and distributor grew 22% in size from 2021, the third largest increase among the top 100 companies in the Fortune 500.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: The coronavirus chewed through Sysco’s core grub-supplying business as restaurants around the world shuttered last year. Revenues for Sysco, America’s biggest wholesale food distributor, fell 12% year on year to $52.9 billion, a decline that caused it to slide 20 places in the Global 500 rankings. COVID-19 took a bite out of profits, too, causing a stomach-churning 87% drop to $215 million. The Houston, Texas-based company pivoted amid pandemic-related closures to help its eatery customers offer alternative options, like takeout-meal kits and contactless menus. But Sysco’s financial prospects are mostly tied to people’s desire to dine out again as the economy reopens.

While the Houston company took in $60.1 billion in 2019, up 2.4% from the year prior, it slid seven places in the Global 500 rankings. Rising food costs, due to inflation and international tariffs, plus higher labor expenses, exacerbated by a shortage of commercial truck drivers, gnawed at the bottom line. Regardless, Sysco grew profits by 17% to $1.6 billion, partly through layoffs, subsidiary consolidation in France, and facility closures in Canada and Europe. companyRankingLists.itemDescription: American Express has built its success as a globally integrated payments company through its connected workplace, the core of which consists of informal “coffee chats” that bolster employee collaboration, increase their visibility, and provide feedback to supervisors. This transparency and consistent employee input has proved vital in sustaining the Amex Flex hybrid and remote work system. Doubling its amount of free annual counseling sessions, Amex continues to expand its mental health services and also provides employee dependent care, eldercare, and support for parents of children with disabilities. Amex has maintained 100% pay equity for four years running and has exceeded its initial goal of providing, by 2024, capital and financial education to over 250,000 businesses run by underrepresented owners. Beyond sustaining connection and support within the company, Amex has pledged more than $30 million through 2024 as part of its Backing Small initiative to support economically vulnerable small business owners through grant programs, mentoring support, and technical assistance.

Archer Daniels Midland (ADM) produces industrial ingredients as varied as high-fructose corn syrup and the cotton cellulose pulp used to make paper. It also runs a commodities trading operation for goods like grain and corn.

  • ADM’s ag services division, which sells seeds for industrial agriculture, had a strong year. Its revenue surged 18.7%, and operating income soared 58% as constrained supplies kept prices of commodities like corn, wheat, and soybeans high.

  • Meanwhile, ADM’s nutrition business, which produces goods from livestock feed to food coloring, proved a drag on company performance: Sales grew just 6.5%, a sluggish pace the company attributed to global currency fluctuations and lower consumption amid rising inflation.

  • In August 2022 ADM entered a joint venture with South Korean chemical company LG Chem to produce sustainable bioplastics in the U.S.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: The Chicago-based agricultural processor’s business spans 200 countries and touches everything from animal feed and human food to cosmetics, alcohol, and paint. Its annual performance has much to do with market conditions and commodity prices: In 2020, sales dipped 0.5% due to lower sales volumes of rice, ethanol, oils, and corn by-products. (ADM idled some facilities because of decreased demand last year.) Still, profits increased 28.5% over the previous year owing to more robust global trade—particularly between the U.S. and China—and strong demand for specialty ingredients like probiotics and plant-based proteins.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: ADM has been on a quest to turn plants into meat substitutes since the 1950s, and claims the title of inventor of the soy veggie patty. Today, as a $64 billion ingredient company supplying global food brands, it may be the biggest plant-based protein producer you’ve never heard of. Its 10 joint ventures and investments in the category range from growing meat from animal cells to creating protein through fermentation to building the world’s largest insect protein production facility (it’s designed to convert flies into animal feed). These deals are key to ADM’s effort to remake itself into more than an agri-giant processor of commodity crops. ADM expects the $10 billion plant-protein sector to triple in size over the next decade as consumers become more concerned about the impact of their diets on the environment.

Both were challenged by lower sales volumes and commodity price declines. A bright spot was the company’s nutrition business, where sales were up 50%, largely due to acquisitions including that of Neovia, a French animal nutrition company.

"MetLife truly cares about your overall well-being. I've been with the company for 15 years, and when I had a health scare last year, management sprang into action and with my grateful agreement, put me into a role within the same department that gave me more flexibility to truly focus on healing. companyRankingLists.title: Fortune 100 Best Companies to Work For
companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
In 2021, MetLife introduced a floating cultural heritage holiday to give employees the flexibility to choose when and how to celebrate their own ethnicity. In 2022, the firm debuted an associated calendar, Moments That Matter, enabling staff to highlight key cultural events, learn about colleagues’ backgrounds, and find opportunities for allyship. The company also introduced custom skin tones and the option to add personalized pronouns and name pronunciation for staff participating in the myMetLife online community.
 

MetLife’s digitally enabled AI learning platform, MyLearning, allows employees to select specific skills they want to develop or use keywords to find already available content that will help them meet their goals. Boasting more than 300,000 assets to date, the platform was used by 73% of staff in 2023.
 

MetLife’s annual Employee Benefit Trends Study yields data the firm has used to demonstrate that a focus on the holistic well-being of workers yields higher levels of productivity, job satisfaction, loyalty, and engagement. Fueled by this research, MetLife aims to create a caring culture throughout the organization.

The global financial services company is implementing innovative employee engagement programs to help achieve its diversity, inclusion, and impact goals.

  • MetLife has committed to investing $2.5 billion in DEI initiatives by 2030. In 2022, the company joined The Hispanic Promise, hosted the Triangle Tech X Conference aimed at lowering barriers for women in STEM, and issued a grant to Syracuse University’s Lender Center for Social Justice to research the origins of the racial wealth gap.

  • One of its DEI initiatives includes the Global DEI Leadership Council, which holds teams across the international company accountable to DEI goals.

  • MetLife’s internal MyPath platform helps employees connect with managers outside of their teams to grow into new roles while contributing to important work.

  • In 2023, MetLife is adding cancer support, digestive health support, family building support, and expanded mental health support for employees on the company health plan.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: MetLife is the largest life insurance provider in the U.S. and serves 100 million customers in nearly 50 countries. MetLife’s revenues for 2021 were up almost 5% over 2020, to $71.1 billion, and profits rose 21.2%, as strong gains in the insurer’s investment portfolio helped offset the impact of high payouts for deaths related to COVID-19. In 2022, MetLife announced diversity, equity, and inclusion commitments that include spending $5 billion with diverse suppliers by 2030 and committing $150 million in funding through the MetLife Foundation to support underserved and underrepresented communities over that same time span.

companyRankingLists.description: Total revenue for the world’s biggest companies fell 4.8% to $31.7 trillion this year—the first decline in half a decade.
companyRankingLists.title: Fortune Global 500
companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Like many insurers, MetLife felt the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on a financial level. Claims and payouts for life insurance policyholders rose as millions around the world died from COVID-19; a decrease in claims related to dental, property, and auto insurance, with customers stuck at home, wasn’t enough to counter the financial impact of those tragedies. Overall, revenues fell 2.6% to $67.8 billion, while profits dropped 8.3% from 2019. But if any business takes the long view, it’s insurance; in fact, at 153 years old, MetLife is one of the rare companies functioning today that also weathered the 1918 flu pandemic. CEO Michel Khalaf now says, “The worst impact of the pandemic on our business performance is behind us.”

companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
The U.S.’s largest health care facility operator reported a decrease in profit and revenue growth in 2022 versus the year prior, partly due to the phasing out of government assistance that accompanied the pandemic.

  • HCA Healthcare, which operates in 20 states in the U.S., has in aggregate removed hospitals from its portfolio and added outpatient surgery centers since 2020, reflecting a broader shift to outpatient care among hospital conglomerates.

  • The health care giant has struggled with staffing issues, like many in the industry, employing higher-cost temporary staffing during the pandemic’s onset. A survey conducted by union researchers found that HCA staffed its hospitals at 30% below the national average in 2020. Responding to the survey, HCA said that its staffing was “safe, appropriate," and “in line” with its industry.

  • The company has repeatedly fought with the Federal Trade Commission over its acquisition of more hospitals, first in Utah in June 2022, and then in Louisiana in April 2023.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Tennessee-based national health care facility operator HCA Healthcare retains its 2021 position after a year that saw profits rise to nearly $59 billion from $51.5 billion. The company was called into action multiple times throughout 2021 as COVID-19 waves swept the country and sent hospital visits ticking upward. HCA has faced criticism in some areas of the country from consumer advocates who contend that it has boosted profits at its hospitals during the pandemic by reducing staffing and services; HCA says that such changes haven’t affected the quality of care. In the first months of 2022, HCA has received 2.1% more same-facility admissions relative to 2021 and 14.6% more emergency room visits.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: As with many other hospital companies, Nashville, Tenn.-based HCA Healthcare faced considerable financial pressure related to the pandemic, suspending its quarterly dividend last spring. Admissions to its hospitals dropped 4.7% for the year owing to fewer procedures and less emergency-room traffic. COVID-19 cases in 2020 made up about 8% of its hospitals’ overall admissions. But HCA finished the year strong: It brought in annual revenue of $51.5 billion, a hair above the previous year’s tally, as revenue per hospitalized patient increased 10.5%. Net income attributable to the company rose 7.1% to nearly $3.8 billion, compared with $3.5 billion in 2019.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
Weapons manufacturer Lockheed Martin had a disappointing year in 2022 as revenue and operating profit both declined, 1.6% and 8.5% respectively. In his 2022 letter to shareholders, CEO James Taiclet attributed the lackluster performance to continued “pandemic impacts and supply-chain challenges,” saying he expected the company to return to sustained growth in 2024.

  • In early 2022, Lockheed Martin canceled a planned $4.4 billion acquisition of rocket engine manufacturer Aerojet, several weeks after the Federal Trade Commission sued to block the deal for violating antitrust regulations.

  • Later in 2022, the Chinese government sanctioned the company for selling weapons to Taiwan, barring Lockheed from importing goods or making new investments in China.

  • The armsmaker inked deals worth a combined $37.8 billion with the U.S. government, its biggest customer, for its signature F-35 fighter jet.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: 2021 was a year of mixed fortunes for defense manufacturer Lockheed Martin. Net income dropped 8% to $6.3 billion, as earnings took a hit when the company had to fund a pension settlement charge of $1.7 billion during the third quarter. But Lockheed Martin was still able to bump up net sales for the year by 2.5%, largely driven by deliveries of 142 F-35 combat aircraft, up from 120 the previous year. The F-35 accounts for around one-quarter of the company’s revenue.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Lockheed Martin launched to new heights in 2019, as revenues grew 11.3% and profits 23.5%, and its stock climbed nearly 50%. Particularly notable was the continued success of the F-35 program: Lockheed delivered 134 of the fighters in 2019, and won new contracts including a Pentagon buy of 478 of the advanced jets for $34 billion. That adds to a production backlog that now sits at $144 billion, much larger than those of competitors. Despite global headwinds in early 2020, Lockheed’s operations haven’t yet shown signs of a stall; the company in July announced Q2 2020 earnings that beat expectations. The company is now being helmed by a new corporate pilot: James Taiclet, who was formerly the chief executive of American Tower, a real estate investment trust. Taiclet succeeds Marillyn Hewson, the top-ranked executive on Fortune's Most Powerful Women in Business list in 2018 and 2019, who stepped down as CEO in June. She will remain as Lockheed's executive chairman.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Lockheed launched to new heights in 2019. Revenues grew 11.3% and profits 23.5%, making it the most profitable aerospace company on the 500. Its stock climbed nearly 50%—well ahead of the robust returns of the broader market. Particularly notable was the continued success of the F-35 program, which for a time risked becoming a costly boondoggle. After producing 91 of the fighters in 2018, Lockheed delivered 134 in 2019, and won new contracts including a Pentagon buy of 478 of the advanced jets for $34 billion. That adds to a production backlog that now sits at $144 billion, much larger than those of competitors. Despite global headwinds in early 2020, Lockheed’s operations haven’t yet shown signs of a stall—with first-quarter net earnings up slightly year over year, guidance for the year barely lowered, and a fresh $6.1 billion Pentagon contract for Patriot missiles.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: New York Life, which jumps 28 spots on the Global 500 this year, was well prepared for COVID-19. Investments will run the gamut from small businesses to affordable housing.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: In December New York Life Insurance entered into a $6.3 billion deal to acquire Cigna’s group life and disability insurance business. Deals that large have been a rarity for the 175-year-old company. Already one of the nation’s largest mutual life insurance firms, New York Life posted a 14% year-over-year profit increase in 2019. The company believes the coronavirus pandemic and its negative impact on the economy are pushing people to think more about their finances—which could ultimately boost New York Life’s insurance offerings.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
Capital One places a high value on education: It expanded its education assistance benefits program in 2022, offering to cover associates’ tuition costs upfront and partnering with Bright Horizons FastTrack to provide general education courses that can be put toward earning a bachelor’s degree at a $1,300 annual flat rate. Participation increased by nearly a quarter within one month. Capital One also partners with 11 HBCUs and Hispanic-serving institutions; it has invested over $1.6 million in scholarships and donations to these schools and hosted programs and events to engage with students and broaden its talent pool.

 

The Catalyst Rotational Program connects employees working in operations and call centers with other business roles, offering a pair of yearlong training initiatives that expose workers to professional development opportunities across the company’s different verticals.
 

Finance is a powerful tool enabling Capital One to advance its social objectives: In 2022, it spent $984 million on diverse suppliers, almost 14% of its procurable spending (and a $280 million increase from the year prior). That spending supported $722.1 million in wages and 8,770 jobs.

  • Capital One is following through on its commitment to create a more diverse and inclusive workforce by launching an Executive Education Program for all U.S. leadership with a focus on the historical and systemic issues that contribute to societal inequality affecting Black and Hispanic communities.

  • In 2022, the company launched a business resource group to support associates who are balancing careers and caregiving.

  • Capital One expanded its Invest in Yourself Day initiative, providing one day each month for associates to practice self-care.

  • Nine out of 10 employees say they are offered “training or development” to further their career goals.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: The pandemic posed an immediate conundrum for bank branches that needed to provide services while keeping employees safe. Capital One, like other banks, implemented safety measures, but the firm also temporarily increased hourly wages, boosting pay by $10 an hour for branch and Capital One Café employees and adding $5 an hour for call center agents. U.S. nonexempt hourly workers, meanwhile, were still paid for all their hours even if they had to pare down their schedules or couldn’t work remotely. That has all helped the credit card titan based in McLean, Va., jump 15 spots on Fortune’s list this year. Remarks one employee: “Sure, it’s just a bank, but it’s run by people who haven’t lost sight of the people in it or the people who are our customers.”

companyRankingLists.description: Total revenue for the world’s biggest companies fell 4.8% to $31.7 trillion this year—the first decline in half a decade.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Having emphasized a move toward tech-enabled digital banking in recent years, Capital One was able to rely on its fintech services amid a pandemic-disrupted 2020. “Our long-standing strategic choices put us in a strong position to respond to both the near-term challenges and the emerging opportunities,” CEO Richard Fairbank said of the bank’s investment in its digital infrastructure. Still, the company’s results were not immune to 2020’s macro headwinds; Capital One saw its revenues fall more than 6% last year, while profits slipped 51%.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
The insurance provider fell 18 spots on this year’s list as its revenue and profits both declined in 2022 from the year prior.

  • The insurance company’s revenue fell to $51 billion in 2022, down 3% from the year prior.

  • Its profits took a nosedive in 2022. It lost $1.3 billion, a drop of 182% from the previous year. The company reported a net loss of $310 million in the fourth quarter in 2022 alone.

  • CEO Tom Wilson blamed the rising cost of auto claims for the company’s losses. Many auto insurance companies struggled as auto claims became more expensive due to inflation and the increased cost of auto parts.

image.title: G500-2020-263-Allstate
image.caption: An Allstate Corp. Milewise device is plugged into the OBD-II port of a vehicle in Northbrook, Illinois, U.S., on Tuesday, Jan. 21, 2020. For more than a decade, auto insurers have had ways to watch a driver's behavior, often using phone apps or so-called telematic devices that connect to a vehicle and send data to the insurers. Now, Allstate, is going a step further by translating the data into an insurance rate that can vary from week to week. Photographer: Christopher Dilts/Bloomberg via Getty Images

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Allstate rebounded well in 2019 after the challenges of the previous year, when Hurricane Michael and the historic California wildfires resulted in higher payouts and a 29% decline in profit. Fewer catastrophe claims helped the Northfield Township, Ill. insurer climb 45 spots in the Global 500 rankings this year. Revenues rose 12% year-over-year, to $44.7 billion, while net income, aided by increased premiums, grew a substantial 133%, to $4.7 billion. CEO Tom Wilson has also attributed the profit surge to cost-cutting measures and increased investment in technology. One example of the latter: a new identity-theft protection product called Digital Footprint, which allows customers to view all websites with accounts that have their personal information, and helps them track data breaches that might affect them.

image.caption: A Caterpillar wheel loader is secured onto a truck at Ideal Tractor in West Sacramento, California, US, on Monday, Aug. 1, 2022. Caterpillar Inc. is scheduled to release earnings figures on August 2.
image.credit: David Paul MorrisBloomberg via Getty Images

companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
The 100-year-old construction equipment company rose five spots in 2023 from No. 73 last year. In the 2022 fiscal year, Caterpillar’s sales and revenue rose 16.6% to $59.4 billion, marking one of the best years in company history.

  • Caterpillar moved its global headquarters from Deerfield, Ill., to Irving, Texas, in 2022.

  • To cope with inflation and increasing costs, Caterpillar raised its equipment prices, which helped boost its sales.

  • But the heavy-machinery maker still had its fair share of struggles in 2022 in the form of COVID-era supply-chain snarls, inflationary forces, and slow pickup in Chinese demand.

  • In October 2022, Caterpillar waived an internal policy that would have required CEO Jim Umpleby to retire when he turns 65, allowing him to continue as the top executive.

  • The company is the world’s leading manufacturer of construction and mining equipment, off-highway diesel and natural gas engines, industrial gas turbines, and diesel-electric locomotives, and now has roughly 60% of its operations outside the U.S.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Big Blue, based in Armonk, N.Y., was early to the AI game with Watson, which was first introduced over two decades ago, mesmerizing the world with what the tech could do. In 2023, the company launched its generative AI offerings, called Watsonx, with the conviction that the technology will bring about a productivity boom. CEO Arvind Krishna expects close to a third of current roles at the company can be taken over by AI and automation in the next five years, freeing up human staff for high-value work. The benefits from boosting productivity could mean reinvestment and larger margins, Krishna suggested. For its part, IBM’s Watsonx already has clients like NASA and Wix on board. The company also brings AI to clients to assist them with automation, modernization, and providing customer care services. For instance, Brazilian bank Bradesco automated its customer service answers using Watson Assistant, responding to 283,000 questions monthly. IBM is focusing on expanding the use of its AI where it is scalable and relevant, while strengthening its position beyond a legacy IT business; it has committed to training 2 million people in AI over the next three years. It acquired software company Apptio in a $4.6 billion deal to complement its AI portfolio and Red Hat cloud business.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Big Blue was under new leadership in 2020 after Arvind Krishna took over for Ginni Rometty as CEO just after the pandemic shut down IBM offices around the world. Adding some of the most rigorous safety measures, IBM has not had a single known case of workplace transmission of COVID-19. The company also offered additional weeks of paid emergency leave for employees dealing with the pandemic and backup child and elder care options. IBM also joined with the U.S. government and other researchers attacking COVID-19 and provided free access to its supercomputers. IBM also reached out to offer resources to historically Black colleges and universities, and CEO Krishna backed specific legislative recommendations for Congress to address racial justice. The company’s “dedication to diversity seems to be consistently reflected in programs and initiatives, rather than just in statements of support,” an employee said. “Actions follow words in meaningful ways.”

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: International Business Machines’ big news in 2020 was the promotion of 30-year company executive Arvind Krishna to the CEO job, succeeding Ginni Rometty. IBM stock has been in a long swoon since 2013, even as the overall market has rocketed; the company needs a revised strategy, and Krishna has wasted little time pursuing one. In October 2020, he announced plans to spin off the business that manages IT infrastructure for other companies—IBM stock rose on the news—and he has been acquiring smaller businesses to build up IBM’s strength in cloud software for business automation. His strategic direction is no surprise; he had been following it even before he was CEO, championing IBM’s acquisition of the Red Hat enterprise software firm in 2019. Judging his success so far is difficult because the pandemic muddied comparisons with past performance.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: In 2019 IBM took the most dramatic step yet in its years-long project of adapting to a fast-changing tech environment, one in which Big Blue's historic dominance has been steadily eroded. In its largest acquisition ever, IBM spent $34 billion to buy Red Hat, the main distributor of the open-source operating system Linux. But progress on the company's top priorities—cloud computing, social engagement, mobile devices, and data analytics—has remained frustratingly slow, with revenue shrinking by 3% in 2019. This spring, however, the venerable computer giant got a new leader to take it forward. In April 2020, Arvind Krishna took the reins as CEO from Ginny Rometty, who had been serving in the role since 2012 and who remains executive chairman.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly is known for breaking ground in insulin, polio vaccines, penicillin, and antidepressants, most famously developing Prozac. Now, in the age of GLP-1 medications, which have transformed obesity and diabetes treatment, the company has shown it can move fast. Eli Lilly brought tirzepatide (sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound) from clinic to market in six years, compared with the company’s usual 11-year development cycles. An ongoing battle for Lilly, as well as Novo Nordisk, involves fighting copycat versions of its GLP-1 products made by compounders, and forcing them to modify their disputed claims. The FDA has warned patients and health care professionals about the dangers of compounded GLP-1 drugs and unapproved weight-loss medicine.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: The pharmaceutical giant was founded in Indianapolis in 1876. It introduced the world's first commercially available insulin product, Iletin, in 1923 for the treatment of diabetes. It was also the first company to manufacture and globally distribute Jonas Salk's polio vaccine. Today Lilly is known best for clinical depression drugs Prozac (1986) and Cymbalta (2004) and antipsychotic medication Zyprexa (1996), though its biggest revenue drivers are diabetes drugs Trulicity (2014) and Humalog (1996). companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
New Jersey–based pharmaceutical company Merck climbed 36 spots from No. 98 on last year’s Best Companies list, with about 75% of the company’s employees worldwide undergoing a pay equity study as of 2021, which grew to 90% in 2022. That 2022 study, by the way, showed that Merck had achieved over 99% pay equity for both women and men and white and non-white employees in the U.S.
 

Merck’s diversity programs have worked to address gender pay disparities and representation of women in the workplace. The company’s board of directors has more gender diversity than the industry norm, consisting of 46% female representation, while women make up 33% of Merck’s executives. Merck’s Women’s Leadership Program and Emerging Women’s Leadership program provide professional development training for women employees.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
While Merck’s business focus revolves around using science to save lives and improve physical health, the company has made the mental health of its employees a priority as well.

  • Roughly 4,000 managers have been trained on how to connect their workers with well-being resources and educated on how to respond with compassion toward someone who may be struggling.

  • Roughly 100 workers have completed Mental Health First Aid training and are available to help colleagues access mental health information and resources. It’s a grassroots project to reduce the stigma and raise awareness of mental health issues.

  • Lyra, launched in 2021, ensures both employees and their families have quick access to high-quality evidence-based mental health care.

  • Employees are provided with a membership to relaxation app Calm, as well as a flex day, time off to volunteer, and a generous parental leave program.

  • “Merck shows that we are people, not just employees, with lives outside of work and honors that and promotes balancing work/home life,” said one worker.

The pharmaceutical firm that makes commonly used drugs, including HPV vaccine Gardasil, has held strong in its 69th year on the Fortune 500 list.

  • Merck surpassed expectations in 2022, bringing in $59.3 billion in revenue and $14.5 billion in profit.

  • In April 2023, Merck announced plans to acquire Prometheus Biosciences for $10.8 billion. It is one of a few deals of its kind, but analysts say it could signal the beginning of a period of intense M&A for biotech companies.

  • Merck, along with Moderna, is making progress toward a cancer vaccine for melanoma patients. The immunotherapy drug Keytruda, Merck’s top seller, is part of the vaccine and was a strong growth driver.

  • Sales of the COVID oral antiviral drug Lagevrio reported robust sales in 2022, but the company expects a significant slowdown in 2023.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Merck’s Gardasil is a potent vaccine against HPV, a sexually transmitted disease that can cause cervical cancer. But until recently, cost and production constraints limited its reach. Merck has now committed more than $1 billion to expand capacity, with a focus on underserved countries. Merck more than doubled global supply of Gardasil between 2017 and 2020 and is on track to do so again by 2023.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Pharmaceutical company Merck fell six spots on the list in its first year with CEO Robert Davis at the helm. But that modest slide masks a successful year in which profits jumped 85%, to $13 billion. Excluding revenue from Organon, the women’s health company whose spinoff was completed in June 2021, Merck’s sales overall increased 17%, including a 20% gain for the company’s hallmark cancer drug Keytruda and a 44% increase in sales for HPV vaccine Gardasil. Merck also registered nearly $1 billion in sales for molnupiravir, an oral antiviral treatment for COVID that received emergency use authorization from the FDA in December 2021.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: New to our list this year, this 130-year-old pharma giant has long devoted itself to the mission: “Save and improve lives.” Though Merck shelved its own vaccine development, President Biden announced in March that the company would help produce J&J’s one-shot COVID vaccine. When current CEO Ken Frazier departs at the end of June, CFO Robert Davis will take the reins. Employees say that during a difficult year, it meant a lot that Merck managed to increase benefits to employees. That included the addition of “LifeCare” specialists who can provide help in hiring a nanny or search for virtual tutors to support e-learning.The company has “stepped up,” notes an employee.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Merck spent much of 2020 developing and testing two COVID-19 vaccine candidates but abandoned the projects in January. The company said in March that it would support the manufacturing and supply of Johnson & Johnson’s COVID-19 vaccine instead. Merck’s worldwide sales increased 2% to $48 billion last year, led by a 30% increase in revenue ($14.4 billion) from its flagship cancer drug Keytruda. Despite the sales growth, Merck saw a 28% decrease in net income in 2020 compared with the prior year. And the numbers in 2021 aren’t exactly flashing green—at least so far: First-quarter sales were flat, and profit declined because of the continuing effects of the pandemic as well as increased competitive pressures for key Merck products. One more challenge for the venerable drugmaker: In June, longtime CEO Ken Frazier steps down after a stellar decade-long run leading the company. He will hand the reins to CFO Robert Davis.

Nationwide builds its workforce with an initial focus on internships—a key pipeline for recruiting diverse entry-level employees. (In 2022, more than half of all interns were ethnically diverse, and over half were women.) Once entry-level workers join the company, the Mentorwide program offers them opportunities to network, build skills, and invest in their career development. Since the program was launched in July 2022, nearly 3,500 associates have participated, 62% of whom are women and 31% of whom are racially or ethnically diverse. 
 

Nationwide offers its associates and members of their households up to 16 free, confidential counseling sessions annually. The program has proved popular, with 27% of employees taking advantage last year compared with an industry norm of 6%. 
 

The company makes an effort to get involved with local communities, partnering with organizations such as Feeding America and the Red Cross; it contributed $3.55 million to those two organizations alone in 2022.

Founded almost a century ago, the Columbus-based insurance giant is among the most diversified insurance and financial services companies in the world. Nationwide offers a wide range of insurance plans for cars, pets, farms, and commercial purposes, as well as mutual funds and retirement plans.

  • Nationwide said 2022 was one of its strongest years ever as its revenue rose to $51 billion, up nearly 9% compared with the previous year. But its 2022 profits of nearly $1 billion marked a 39% drop from 2021.

  • Already the largest pet insurance provider in the country, Nationwide partnered with Petco Health, a pet-focused wellness company, to expand its services in the sector.

  • In April 2022, Nationwide increased its minimum wage to $21 an hour, one of the highest in the U.S.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Nationwide employees know it’s more than just an insurance company with a catchy jingle: It’s a place where they can grow their careers. Since 2020, the company has invested $160 million in its Future of Work Center, a five-year program focused on upskilling and reskilling Nationwide’s associates. Diversity, equity, and inclusion is also a big companywide initiative, which includes programming like Cultural Fluency in the Workplace, which helps workers develop cross-cultural acumen when interacting with people from diverse cultural backgrounds and varied perspectives. “I specifically love the sense of community obligation and treating people as a whole being and not just a skill set,” says an employee. Development opportunities abound for those who work in the office, as well as for the 50% of employees who routinely work from home, and Nationwide makes an effort to keep remote workers connected to the company’s culture.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Founded in 1926 as a small auto insurer, Nationwide Mutual Insurance is now one of the country’s more diversified financial services companies: Its products include car, motorcycle, homeowners, pet, farm, life, and commercial insurance as well as annuities, mutual funds, retirement plans, and specialty health services. The company reported record-high total sales and premiums in 2021, as year-over-year revenue grew 13%. Nationwide also invested $350 million in financial and insurance startups in 2021. It expanded its eco-friendly portfolio over the course of the year, too, investing $173 million in renewable energy and $375 million in green bonds. The company says its own carbon footprint has decreased by almost 40% per square foot since 2010.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: As lockdowns kicked in, the share of the insurer’s workforce who worked remotely soared from 20% to 98%—in just over a week. Nationwide managed the transition with a massive dose of support, expanding paid time off for those with caregiving duties and bolstering day-care and educational resources for parents. Above all, management stayed in touch: The company says its “leader communications” rose 500%. That connection helped Nationwide rise 66 spots in our ranking. “Frequently hearing from executives gave me the reassurance to know that we were not alone,” says one associate. Nationwide aims to build on that success post-pandemic, when, it says, about 50% of employees will continue to work from home.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: The insurance giant had a challenging year. Nationwide’s net operating income decreased from $1.9 billion in 2019 to $797 million in 2020. There was also a dip in sales to $41.9 billion in 2020. Low interest rates and changing consumer behaviors were among the factors that put pressure on the company’s sales results, CFO Mark Thresher said in the company’s annual report. New technologies may be paying off, however, as Nationwide saw 30% of new auto-insurance business enrolled in its SmartRide and SmartMiles programs. By 2025, the company expects 70% of all new auto-insurance customers will sign up for policies that allow for a telematics device to be installed in their cars to record driving behavior—and encourage accident-avoidance and cost-saving habits behind the wheel.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
The Atlanta-based carrier moved 28 spots up this year’s list, thanks to a robust travel rebound in the wake of the COVID-era slowdown. Its operating revenue for the year reached $50.6 billion, up 69% from 2021.

  • In May 2022, Delta said it would remove 100 flights a day from its summer schedule to stave off travel chaos as it rebuilt its operations. In the month to follow, however, CEO Ed Bastian apologized for delays and the disruption of hundreds of flights owing in part to understaffing.

  • Delta reached a deal with its pilots’ union in March 2023 to boost pay by 34% over three years.

  • Inflation threatened Delta’s profits in early 2023, but the company anticipates a 2% to 4% nonfuel unit cost decline through the year compared with 2022.

  • Still, Delta faces a pilot shortage and the delayed delivery of new aircraft, which could reduce flight volume and raise airfares.

  • The airline expects flight demand to grow in 2023, which will help offset higher expenses, like the surging cost of fuel and labor.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: In retrospect, 2019 was a halcyon year for the travel industry. Fuel was cheap, travel demand was high, and as the only major U.S. airline without Boeing 737 MAX planes in its fleet, Delta sidestepped the fallout from their grounding. Annual revenue rose 5.8% to $47 billion, and net income jumped 21.1% to $4.8 billion, giving Delta its tenth straight year of profitability—if likely the last it will see for some time. After the pandemic closed down most airline travel and led Delta and its competitors to seek government aid, CEO Ed Bastian predicted that Delta will need at least three years to get back to a sustainable—but still sub-2019—level of travel. As Bastian told Fortune: “This is going to take a long time.”

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: It’s year 27 on the list for this grocery retailer, which operates in Alabama, Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Virginia—and this year opened operations in Kentucky. The company is over 90 years old and currently operates more than 1,365 grocery stores, 370 liquor stores, and 14 stand-alone pharmacies. In September, just under 6,300 associates volunteered to help people facing food insecurity. The company also expanded its paid parental leave policy to allow anyone who has welcomed a new child in their lives an option for paid time off during the first year following birth or adoption.

Staff at Publix tend to stick around, and many see career growth; some 90% of store managers started out working on the floor. Read more: Shoppers are obsessed with Publix and Wegmans. companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Publix Super Markets, founded in 1930, is the largest employee-owned company in the U.S. During the pandemic, the culture around employee ownership has helped Publix to retain employees and keep operations steady at a time when many other grocers have grappled with high turnover. In April 2022, the company's board of directors approved a five-for-one stock split that lowered the price of shares and made it easier for newer employees to buy in. The chain has almost 1,300 stores, primarily in the southeastern U.S., and Publix saw a 7% increase in revenue in 2021. Publix also recently donated more than 50 million pounds of produce as part of an initiative to support farmers and food banks in the Southeast.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
The pharmaceutical giant rode its groundbreaking mRNA COVID-19 vaccine and antiviral pill Paxlovid to record revenue in 2022; the $100.3 billion it raked in (up from $81.3 billion in 2021) catapulted the company 40 spots on this year’s Fortune 500 list.

  • Pfizer is planning to sell its COVID-19 vaccine commercially in 2023, rather than contracting with the U.S. government, with a target price between $110 and $130 per dose.

  • Still, it expects revenue to drop as the demand for COVID vaccines eases in 2023. Pfizer has a slate of other new drugs in its pipeline, such as the Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) vaccine and medication for migraines.

  • The company is expected to lose patent protections for some key drugs, including Ibrance, used for breast cancer treatment, between 2025 and 2030.

  • It has acquired other biotech or smaller pharma companies to bolster its pipeline in the future. Key 2022 deals include the $5.4 billion purchase of Global Blood Therapeutics and the $11.6 billion acquisition of Biohaven.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Pfizer’s role in responding to COVID-19 has returned it to the forefront of the pharmaceutical industry—and helped it climb 34 spots on the Fortune 500 this year. As of April 2022, approximately 3.3 billion Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccines had been shipped to 179 countries, and some 338 million doses had been administered in the U.S. alone. From 2020 to 2021 its revenue nearly doubled, to $81.3 billion, with the vaccine accounting for the bulk of that gain. Pfizer’s oral antiviral pill, Paxlovid, which has been shown to reduce the risk of hospitalization or death from COVID by about 90%, is likely to join the vaccine in boosting its bottom line: As of April 2022, the Biden administration has committed to purchasing 20 million treatment courses of Paxlovid.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: How do you balance being one of the world’s saviors during a pandemic without being perceived as gloating or, more important, gouging a global population in need? That’s the tricky needle Pfizer has had to thread, given the company’s status as one of the most effective coronavirus vaccine manufacturers in the world. Pfizer recorded 2020 revenues of about $42 billion—but that largely excludes the post-winter period, when Pfizer’s COVID vaccine was granted emergency use authorization by the FDA. The company expects to bring in $26 billion in COVID vaccine sales alone this year, about 60% of its total 2020 revenues, thanks to its sprawling relationships with governments and pandemic-focused organizations across the globe. An added benefit? Via its partnership with Germany’s BioNTech, the maker of the “little blue pill” is now synonymous with mRNA vaccine technology that could feed its pipeline in infectious disease treatments and other therapeutics for years to come.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Pfizer slips 17 spots this year, in large part because of the expiration last year of one of its more lucrative patents, for the fibromyalgia drug Lyrica. That eroded the drugmaker's revenue, which fell 4% overall in 2019. But Pfizer also made some big moves: After years of rumors that it would split up, Pfizer finally slimmed down, announcing over the summer that it would merge Upjohn, its off-patent drug division, with general drug company Mylan. Meanwhile, the pharmaceutical giant found some significant efficiencies in its operations: profits surged some 46%. The company, which is developing a promising COVID-19 vaccine in partnership with German drug company BioNTech, in July announced the U.S. government had ordered $1.95 billion worth of doses of the new treatment—to provide it to Americans for free, if the FDA approves the vaccine.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Pfizer slipped a few spots, in large part because of the expiration last year of one of its more lucrative patents, for the fibromyalgia drug Lyrica. That eroded the drugmaker's revenue, which fell 4% overall in 2019. But Pfizer also made some big moves: After years of rumors that it would split up, Pfizer finally slimmed down, announcing over the summer that it would merge Upjohn, its off-patent drug division, with general drug company Mylan. Meanwhile, the pharmaceutical giant found some significant efficiencies in its operations: profits surged some 46%.

The newly created company that helps some of the biggest tech companies—including HP and Google—with IT distribution and cloud solutions leaped to No. 64 on this year’s Fortune 500, up from No. 108.

  • The company owes most of its explosive fiscal-year 2022 revenue growth—97% year over year—to the deal that brought it into its current existence: the merger of Tech Data and SYNNEX Corporation, which was completed in September 2021.

  • Strong demand for data center support, IT infrastructure, and data security drove TD Synnex’s business through 2022, despite supply-chain hiccups and backlogs.

  • TD Synnex serves over 150,000 customers worldwide, and employs close to 24,000 people.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
ConocoPhillips, one of the world’s largest independent oil and gas exploration and production companies, skyrocketed 28 spots up the rankings in 2023, surfing a rise in crude oil prices driven largely by the war in Ukraine.

  • ConocoPhillips revenue rose nearly 70%, and its profits increased 131% in 2022 compared with 2021, when energy companies were still recovering from the dip in oil and gas demand resulting from the pandemic’s effect on travel.

  • Throughout 2022 ConocoPhillips doubled down on liquefied natural gas (LNG), increasing its ownership of LNG operations in Australia, Germany, Qatar, and the U.S. Gulf Coast.

  • In March 2023 President Biden formally allowed ConocoPhillips to drill for oil in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska, the nation’s largest untouched expanse of wilderness, miring the energy giant in a larger controversy over government-sponsored oil and gas drilling projects.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: The Houston-based company is one of the world's largest independent oil and gas exploration and production companies, operating in 14 countries. ConocoPhillips reported profits of $8.1 billion in 2021, and revenue jumped 151% as energy demand soared; the company leaped 79 spots on the Fortune 500. The company began new exploration projects in Canada, Malaysia, and Alaska over the course of the year. Its Alaska operations posed problems in early 2022, however, as a monthlong natural gas leak at its Alpine Oil Field forced a temporary shutdown of drilling and prompted lawmakers and regulators to criticize ConocoPhillips for its slow response.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: The oil and gas company's 29-spot dip in rankings doesn’t tell the full story, given an enduring period of volatility in the crude market. While sales for the year fell 5%, to $36.7 billion, profits shot up 15% year-over-year, as ConocoPhillips tightened its structure and grew daily production volume by 5%. The Houston-based company generated more than $3 billion from the sales of its U.K. and northern Australia businesses, bringing total cash and short-term investments for the year up to $8.4 billion. The refocusing of its portfolio, as well as disciplined spending, allowed ConocoPhillips to reward shareholders with $1.5 billion in dividends and $3.5 billion in share buybacks.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Pharma company AbbVie might not be a household name, despite large revenue numbers, but the 13,000 employees in its 15 European bases are encouraged to develop a sense of belonging and purpose. Considering the company's mission to make a remarkable impact on people's lives through drug and treatment research, it makes sense that AbbVie's workplace culture focuses on employees' physical, mental and emotional health. AbbVie Vitality programs are designed to support employees and encourage healthy eating and movement, provide resources for parenting, caregiving and stress management. Employee events such as AbbVie in Motion provide opportunities to make connections with colleagues while promoting healthy behaviors. Together, AbbVie colleagues around the world logged more than 25 million physical activity minutes during 2024's four-week team challenge. A feeling of wider social purpose is achieved by collaborating with local nonprofits and governments on community assistance programs, philanthropic ventures, and medical support for natural disasters.

Jumping 26 spots from last year’s Best Companies list, global biopharmaceutical company AbbVie abides by the “Your career, your development” professional development paradigm to give employees opportunities for self-guidance in finding a fulfilling career within the company. Its Talent Link proprietary networking platform allows employees to build profiles, highlight skills, and gives other employees access to their profiles to help them job match, find mentors, and earn leadership badges.
 

In October 2023, AbbVie hosted Celebration of Culture, a daylong teamwork- and empowerment-building event. The day started in the earliest relevant time zone, and all events were captioned and available on demand to make them accessible to employees.

AbbVie’s Ability Employee Resource Group introduced NDWorks, a neurodiversity pilot program to raise awareness and foster sustainable solutions to support neurodivergent individuals in the workplace. After continued efforts to advance gender equity in the workplace, AbbVie’s workforce is made up of 56% women, and 52% of management positions are held by women as of December 2022.

One of the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies continues to prioritize its company culture, but the recent expiration of its stranglehold on a marquee drug raises questions about the future of the business.

  • In 2022, AbbVie restructured; however, a spokesperson said layoffs impacted less than 1% of its employees. In January of this year, the company also saw the expiration of its patent on Humira, its best-selling anti-inflammatory medicine and a key portion of its annual revenue.

  • AbbVie has a systematic approach to crafting its corporate ethos. It has a dedicated organizational culture team of six people and a global cohort of 250 AbbVie Way Ambassadors, employees who are tasked with being role models for other staff members.

  • Ways We Work is a companywide creed that’s a blueprint for how staff should work together and treat one another. It was developed after extensive discussions with employees.

  • AbbVie launched an internal program to develop the skill sets of employees from a diverse range of backgrounds.

  • In 2023, AbbVie introduced the formal expectation that higher-ranking employees need to include an inclusion goal among their operational and business plans.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
The pharmaceutical company, spun off from Abbott Laboratories in 2013, dropped 10 spots on this year's Fortune 500, notching a relatively modest 3.3% increase in revenue.

  • Throughout 2023, generic versions of AbbVie’s blockbuster drug, Humira, will become available in the U.S., threatening the near-term sales of the pharmaceutical firm. Humira, which treats various inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, is one of the bestselling drugs in history, and accounted for approximately 37% of AbbVie’s total net revenues in 2022.

  • To prepare for the expiration of Humira’s patent, the company has invested in two other immunological drugs, Skyrizi and Rinvoq. Net revenues from Skyrizi increased 79% year over year on an operational basis, and revenues from Rinvoq increased 55%.

  • The company has also made two recent acquisitions in order to diversify its portfolio, buying Syndesi Therapeutics in March 2022 and DJS Antibodies in October of that year.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
The off-price department store chain brought in nearly $3.5 billion in profits in 2022, a 7% increase over 2021. TJX dropped 12 spots on the Fortune 500 list after a 22-spot jump last year.

  • Marmaxx, TJX’s apparel unit, was its biggest revenue driver, bringing in $30 billion of the $49.9 billion the company generated overall. Its HomeGoods division, however, saw slower sales after two years of expansion during the pandemic.

  • TJX continues to lag in the e-commerce space, which held the company back at COVID’s height.

  • Still, TJX has outlasted many of its competitors; Bed Bath & Beyond’s bankruptcy may lead to more foot traffic at TJX stores.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: TJX is the parent company of off-price retailers like T.J.Maxx, Marshalls, HomeGoods, Sierra, and Homesense, operating almost 4,700 stores in nine countries. The pandemic initially had a severe impact on revenue for TJX, which gets only a small percentage of its sales from e-commerce. But as lockdowns ended, the company rebounded, and in 2021, it grew revenue by 51% year over year, enabling it to jump 22 spots on this year’s list. In March 2022, TJX announced it would sell its 25% stake in Russian apparel retailer Familia in response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. In April 2022, the company announced that it is aiming to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions in its operations by 2040.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
United Airlines, one of the largest American airline carriers by revenue, has jumped 50 spots on this year’s Fortune 500, securing a spot within the top 100.

  • The Chicago-based company benefited from the post-COVID travel rebound, bringing in $45 billion in revenue in 2022, an 83% increase from 2021.

  • United, like its rivals, faced a number of challenges through 2022—from high fuel costs and staffing shortages to delays in airplane deliveries. But the company’s 2022 fourth-quarter profit outstripped Wall Street estimates as consumers proved willing to shell out money to take trips.

  • As travel demand continues to recover, United has purchased 100 new aircraft (with an option to buy 100 more) to support its growth. It also added new routes over the summer, including some that it dropped in previous years. The airline has yet to finalize a new contract with its pilots after five years of negotiations.

  • United’s flight training school, United Aviate Academy, graduated its first class in January 2023, and boasted that 80% of the graduating class was made up of women or people of color.

image.caption: An attendee wearing an eye masks sits in a mock-up of a United Airlines Holdings Inc. Polaris business class seat during an event in Chicago, Illinois, U.S., on Thursday, Oct. 24, 2019. United will fly customers on a new regional jet crafted to its exact specifications on October 27, an aircraft that comes with 10 first class seats. By putting premium perches on a small regional jet with a total of only 50 seats, United hopes to close an amenities gap for a highly competitive group of travelers from smaller cities to its Chicago and Newark, New Jersey hubs. Photographer: Taylor Glascock/Bloomberg via Getty Images

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: United overcame international and aircraft-related challenges to flourish in 2019. Despite the grounding of its Boeing 737 MAX jets and the impact of Hong Kong protests on its flights there, United increased its passenger revenue and benefitted from low fuel costs; overall revenues rose 4.7% to $43.3 billion, and profits jumped 41.3%, to $3 billion. CEO Oscar Munoz, who spent years helping United recover from its troubled merger with Continental, last June dropped the latter’s name from the combined company. J. Scott Kirby, who had been president of the company succeeded Munoz as CEO in May 2020. But the airline’s large international business meant that United was one of the first U.S. carriers to feel the effects of the coronavirus pandemic; by April, it had accepted government aid, slashed capacity, given voluntary unpaid leaves of absence to more than 20,000 workers, and reported $1.7 billion in first-quarter losses. The pain continued in the second quarter as sales plummeted 87% compared to the year before and United reported a loss of $1.6 billion.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Best known for its database software, the venerable Oracle has struggled in recent years with sluggish revenue growth: Total revenue was only 3.6% in 2021, and the company slid down 11 spots on the Fortune 500. companyRankingLists.title: Fortune Global 500
companyRankingLists.itemDescription: The database giant is trying mightily to fight off stagnation. Sales dropped 1% year over year to $39.1 billion, owing in part to Oracle’s cloud unit, which is growing far more slowly than those of rivals Amazon and Microsoft. Last fall, Oracle made a surprising push along with Walmart to acquire the U.S. operations of red-hot TikTok, in a deal championed by former President Donald Trump. But that deal is now reportedly on hold under the Biden administration. In another blow: The U.S. Supreme Court recently sided with Google parent Alphabet over Oracle in a major copyright infringement case involving the use of Java software code.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Cisco is slimming down: Although its headcount has barely budged over the past several years, the digital communications giant announced it would be letting go over 4,000 staff in February of 2024. But it hasn’t let that get in the way of its lofty ESG goals, which employees cite as one of the things they like best about Cisco. The San Jose–based company launched the Cisco Aspire Fund in 2020, through which it’s investing $50 million in startups led by diverse leaders and helping them grow by bringing them into the Cisco ecosystem. The company has committed to hybrid work as part of its long-term workplace model, drafting a set of ground rules on issues such as shared office space and sustainability, and engaging employees in conversations around workplace policies. To attract and retain workers outside traditional urban centers, Cisco is looking at shifting some facilities to smaller, more dispersed locations that are nevertheless easy to access through multiple means of transport, thus enabling customers and partners to visit and teams to collaborate in a hybrid way.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Cisco, like many technology companies, is at an inflection point after letting go of roughly 4,800 workers at the beginning of 2023. Layoffs can hurt even strong company cultures, but the digital communications and technology conglomerate does have a solid foundation that can help it weather the recent upheaval and maintain its No. 1 spot for the third consecutive year. Cisco’s inclusive workplace is built on a strong sense of purpose that comes through in projects like the Purpose Report and ESG Reporting Hub, where the company has been publicly detailing progress on its environmental, social, and governance (ESG) initiatives since 2005.​ Amanda Cumberland, director of ESG strategy and reporting, insights, and impact at Cisco, recently wrote about how proud she is of the difference Cisco makes for people and the world. “We don’t have it all figured out yet, but we want to keep learning and doing more,” she says.

companyRankingLists.title: Change the World
companyRankingLists.itemDescription: One-third of the world’s population remains digitally disconnected, and those most impacted by economic inequality are more likely to lack access. Cisco’s Country Digital Acceleration (CDA) program, established in 2015, aims to address this digital divide. To date, CDA has invested hundreds of millions of dollars in over 1,500 active or completed projects in 49 countries. In the U.S., these projects have included expanding access to free Wi-Fi for approximately 40,000 people in Fort Worth, Tex., and installing broadband services in Orangeburg, S.C., home to two historically black colleges and universities. Abroad, Cisco introduced mobile doctor’s offices for the elderly and refugees in Germany, and helped rural villages get online in India. The good deeds also build business good will: Over the 2023 fiscal year, Cisco says, the CDA project generated a 2,400% return on investment, measured by the dollar amount of incremental bookings for Cisco services and products generated by CDA investments.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: HP Inc., a global provider of computers and printing products, believes that diversity, equity, and inclusion are a business imperative, and has set specific goals related to gender and race in leadership and to closing the digital divide. The company’s Racial Equality and Social Justice Task Force identifies opportunities to reinforce equality in the company by hiring more people of color and minorities, influencing the industry, and advocating for equal opportunities through public policy and civil action. This past year, the company has advocated for federal funding for historically Black colleges and universities, and supported national recognition of and state-level protections for LGBTQ+ marriages. It also offers health care programs, like Black Health, which aims to ensure culturally competent health care and improved health outcomes for Black employees; and LGBTQ+ Health, to help queer-identifying people secure specialized care providers who understand community-specific risks. In 2023, HP created a “Beyond the Spectrum” toolkit to support families and caregivers of people with Autism Spectrum Disorder, offering advice on therapy, complexities of care, and emotional support.

  • Volunteer communities of HP employees, called Business Impact Networks (BINs), are key to attracting and retaining diverse talent. This year, HP launched the Standing Ovation Awards to acknowledge the contributions of the different BINs.

  • The “Hire EQ: Equitable hiring for better outcomes” training program teaches managers to create a more diverse pipeline and create a better experience for all employees to grow.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: In 2022, HP was the only tech company to receive A ratings from the Carbon Disclosure Project for its sustainability efforts, including reaching zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2040 and counteracting deforestation for non-HP paper products used in its printers by 2030. HP jumped from No. 9 in the 2022 Modern Board 25 ranking to seven this year. Outgoing Levi Strauss CEO Chip Bergh has helmed HP’s board since 2017, bringing experience in consumer goods as the tech company doubles down on consumer electronics since its 2015 decoupling from Hewlett Packard’s enterprise tech business. Notable board members include Bruce Broussard, CEO of health care company Humana; Stacy Brown-Philpot, former CEO of TaskRabbit; and Judith Miscik, CEO of geopolitical consulting firm Kissinger Associates and former CIA deputy director of intelligence. After a 2022 net revenue drop of 0.8% year over year, the company announced a cost-cutting plan to save $1.4 billion through 2025, including 6,000 employee layoffs over the next three years. Forty-six percent of HP’s 13-person board (12 of whom are independent) are members of underrepresented groups, and 46% are women.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
HP focuses on consumer technology, in contrast to fellow Hewlett-Packard corporate scion Hewlett Packard Enterprise, No. 2 on this list, which focuses on enterprise tech. HP scored a major coup in April 2022 when Warren Buffett’s holding company, Berkshire Hathaway, disclosed a $4.2 billion, 11% stake in the company—a vote of confidence in its long-term strategy that caused its stock price to soar.

HP’s board scored well for gender equality, age dispersion, and board independence. Chip Bergh, the CEO of Levi Strauss, has been the board chair at HP since 2017. Board member Bruce Broussard is CEO of Humana and former chief of McKesson Specialty/US Oncology.

Other former CEOs on the board include Shumeet Banerji (Booz & Company) and Robert R. Bennett (Discovery and Liberty Media). Stephanie A. Burns is the former CEO of Dow Corning and also sits on the board of Corning, as well as food manufacturer Kellogg.

Stacy Brown-Philpot is the former CEO of TaskRabbit and was previously entrepreneur-in-residence at Google, in addition to holding multiple leadership roles at the tech giant. She’s also on the investment committee of the SB Opportunity Fund, a venture fund for Black, Latinx, and Native American founders.

Aída Álvarez, former head of the Small Business Administration under President Bill Clinton, is also on the board. Jami Miscik, who joined the board last year, is a former CIA deputy director of intelligence.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: The leading maker of personal computers, printers, and other tech gear, including 3D printing solutions, saw sales take off even as many other companies suffered sinking sales during the pandemic. In a year of crisis, HP reached underserved communities through $21 million in various programs, grants, and donations. These initiatives included producing more than 5 million 3D printed PPE parts to help health care workers, and printing and distributing hundreds of thousands of education booklets for young students and teachers in the U.S., Canada, India, and Haiti. Helping its workers at home meant of course providing the right technology but also not overlooking small conveniences like starting meetings five or 10 minutes after each hour to give stressed parents time to check in with their kids learning at home. “I really appreciate that so much thought and care was put into our health and well-being from the get-go,” one employee says.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: The personal computer and printing giant relies on plastics for many of its products—and an ever-growing share of those plastics is recycled. companyRankingLists.itemDescription: While HP’s sales held steady last year, its profits plunged 41%. The company's biggest highlight in recent months was its successful defense against a hostile takeover bid by copy-machine giant Xerox, initiated in the fall. Xerox executives pitched the deal as a way to create a printing powerhouse while opening up the door to cost-cutting. Ultimately, the coronavirus and its impact on the economy forced Xerox to call off its takeover bid.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Charter Communications, the Stamford, Conn.–based telecommunications giant, dropped five spots on this year’s list. Though it added 1.2 million new internet customers over the course of the year, the company continued to see declines in residential video customers, losing 71,000 in the last quarter of 2021 alone. Still, its revenue increased 7.5% to $51.7 billion, and its profits increased a more dramatic 44.5% to $4.7 billion. In February 2022, the company announced a new $20 standard minimum wage in the face of a continued tight labor market.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: The Connecticut-based telecom giant added a record 2.2 million new Internet customers in its most recent fiscal year. That helped the company bring in $48 billion in revenue, a 5% increase from the year before. Net income also grew significantly—an impressive 93% jump year over year. But the number of video subscribers barely budged. That wasn’t a big surprise, given the continuing cord-cutting trend and the plethora of nontraditional options viewers now have for consuming content. Charter’s average monthly revenue from residential customers was also challenged, dipping slightly from $112.63 per month in 2019 to $111.15 in 2020.
